- 2026-08-29T17:41:10.916Z — rule: **An adapter never reports record state: wrote_back and the launched session's identity are derived from the fold, and when several candidate sessions exist the driver records a stall rather than guessing.** — chose **Adapter contract details (1.3): an adapter is a process wrapper and nothing more. launch(request) returns a handle with usage(), optional nudge(), kill() and wait(); capabilities {usage, nudge, model, effort} are declared up front and the threshold policy is REFUSED on an adapter lacking usage or nudge (policyUnavailable), so usage() is optional in effect — fx reports no tokens and still runs the task policy identically. wrote_back is DERIVED from the fold (wroteBack: the session is registered and carries a summary), never reported by the adapter. - 2026-08-29T18:02:10.005Z — rule: **Driver handoff reasons are derived from the fold — needs_user is the named task in status `blocked`, task_done needs a write-back AND a terminal task status; never infer a reason from write-back prose or an exit code.** — chose **Handoff reasons are read STRUCTURALLY from the fold, never from write-back prose (2.2). needs_user = the task the driver named is `blocked` after the session — a status that already requires a note, so the operator's question is recorded where the next reader looks. task_done = the session wrote back AND some task reached a terminal status (done or dropped). Everything else is a stall, including a session that finished work but skipped its write-back: the next session resumes from the next_action, so an unwritten session leaves the queue exactly where it was. The prompt states the blocked lever verbatim, so the agent triggers the stop deliberately instead of the driver inferring it.** over Matching next_action prose for "ask the user"/"operator"/"decide"; a new needs_user event; treating any task status change (pending→active) as progress; trusting the adapter's exit code as the verdict. because A prose matcher would assert a state it never tested — the shape D3 already rejected for wrote_back and 3c909f0 for liveness — and it would silently mis-stop on wording the driver's author never imagined. `blocked` is the record's existing word for "wants to happen, cannot yet", carries a mandatory reason, and is visible to every surface without new schema. Requiring the write-back for task_done keeps the two halves of a handoff honest: the queue only truly advanced when the record says both that the task closed and what the next session should do.
- 2026-08-29T18:02:20.697Z — rule: **`sofar drive` never creates or destroys a git worktree or switches a branch; it launches into one directory for the whole run and refuses to start unless that directory's `.sofar` log for the initiative is the same file it is driving.** — chose **One working directory per RUN, not one worktree per session (2.2, superseding the plan text of 2.2). `sofar drive` launches every session with cwd = the repo root by default, or `--cwd <dir>` for a worktree the OPERATOR made; the driver creates no worktree and switches no branch. Before the first launch it verifies that `<cwd>/.sofar/initiatives/<slug>/events.jsonl` resolves (realpath) to the log it is driving, and refuses otherwise; it also warns when the launch directory's branch binds to a different initiative, since that is the digest the child's SessionStart hook will inject.** over A fresh `git worktree add` per session, as 2.2's plan text says; the driver creating and removing worktrees itself; symlinking `.sofar` into a worktree on the session's behalf. because Sessions in a run are SEQUENTIAL and cumulative — session N+1 continues session N's work — so a fresh checkout per session discards uncommitted work and re-pays every setup cost the tree carries (node_modules above all: a worktree with no install cannot run `npm test`, and the acceptance criteria are tests). Isolation between sessions is not a thing a sequential run needs; isolation from the OPERATOR's tree is, and an operator who wants it can point `--cwd` at a worktree they set up once. The verification is the part that actually matters: the record is committed, so a plain worktree carries a STALE COPY of it, and a session writing there would fork the queue invisibly — realpath equality is the cheap check that catches exactly that.
- 2026-08-29T18:20:41.064Z — chose **Threshold policy mechanics (2.3). `run_started` gains `context_window`, REQUIRED for `threshold` exactly as `threshold_pct` is — a percentage with no denominator names no number of tokens, so a record carrying only the percentage cannot say what the last driver nudged at. Sofar never infers the window from the model name: the operator states it (`--context-window`) and the record keeps it. The nudge lives in one dependency-free module (driver/nudge.ts) that the adapter writes and the PostToolUse hook reads, because the hook is on the 100ms hot path and must not import the spawn surface to learn an env var name. The file's EXISTENCE is the signal and its contents are detail: an unreadable nudge still injects the instruction, without the number. The driver reads the gauge once immediately and then every 2s, and nudges ONCE — the file persists, so the hook re-injects on every later tool call by itself. The prompt differs by policy: `threshold` tells the session to keep taking tasks until nudged, since print mode ends the turn on its own and a session told to do one task makes the gauge decorative. A nudged session that wrote back and resolved a task hands off with reason `threshold`, not `task_done` — the reason names the lever that moved.** over Inferring the window from a per-model table (a table sofar cannot keep true would mis-time every handoff silently); defaulting the window to 200k and leaving it out of the record (the same unreplayable run threshold_pct's rule already forbids); putting the nudge text in the driver and having the hook echo it; re-writing the nudge file on every poll; injecting only once. because The record is the driver's only state (D2), and a resumed run must nudge at the same absolute number of tokens as the one it continues — 80% of 200k and 80% of 1M are two different runs wearing one id, which is why --resume now also refuses to change a run's policy. Keeping the sentence in the hook keeps the instruction where the other injected context lives and lets the file stay a signal rather than a message queue. Tolerance on read is the fold's own rule applied to a one-line file: a half-written nudge must never fail a session.
- 2026-08-29T18:30:13.666Z — rule: **A driven session's permission surface is recorded in `run_started.surface` and its settings file is written, read back and compared at EVERY launch — never assert a surface the record does not carry, and never claim the driver bounds what a session can do, since its file only adds to the operator's own settings sources.** — chose **The permission surface is a RUN property whose FILE is a SESSION artifact (2.4). `run_started` gains an optional `surface` {permission_mode, allow[], deny?, model?, effort?}, recorded once; --resume takes the run's recorded surface over the resuming driver's flags, exactly as it already does for threshold_pct/context_window/max_sessions. The settings FILE is written per session into that session's own temp dir beside the nudge, read back and compared before the spawn — a mismatch throws and the launch never happens. Mode travels as the --permission-mode FLAG, allow/deny in the file: a flag cannot be outranked by a higher-precedence settings source, while lists belong in a file and a file is what can be read back. Default mode is acceptEdits; default allow is exactly what the driver's own prompt orders — mcp__sofar, Bash(sofar:*), and the local git verbs behind "commit code and record together" — and nothing else. No default deny.** over one per-run file written and verified once at run start; putting the mode in the settings file alongside the lists; passing allow/deny as --allowedTools/--disallowedTools argv with no file at all; defaulting the allow-list to a project's test and build commands (npm test, npm run build); shipping a default deny-list of outward-facing verbs (git push, npm publish); and restricting --setting-sources so the driver's file is the only source because Verification is worth only its recency: a file written and read back at run start says nothing about the session launched two hours later, and the adapter already mints a per-session temp dir for the nudge, so the settings file costs nothing extra and is proven at every launch. The mode is the half that must not be silently outranked — print mode cannot prompt, so under `default` mode every gated call fails and every session stalls, which is the bug 2.4 exists to fix; a flag beats every settings source, a settings key does not. A test-command default would be a table sofar cannot keep true (the same reasoning that makes it refuse to infer the context window from a model name), so the project's own needs are the operator's to state with --allow. A default deny is redundant under acceptEdits (Bash is gated by the mode already) and a trap the operator cannot lift under bypassPermissions, where they have explicitly asked for everything — sofar records that surface rather than policing it. --setting-sources is deliberately NOT restricted, verified against this repo: its hooks live in .claude/settings.json (project) and its MCP server enablement in .claude/settings.local.json (local), so a driven session cut off from those could neither receive the record nor call sofar at all. The file is therefore an ADDITIONAL source that can only widen what the operator's own settings allow, and the record says what sofar pinned, never what the session could ultimately do.
- 2026-08-30T04:24:38.086Z — rule: **An adapter declares what it CANNOT do — usage, nudge, permission_rules, cost — and the driver states the consequence on the run's progress stream before the work starts; never let an inert flag (a cost cap that cannot fire, an allow-list the agent cannot express) pass silently into an unattended run.** — chose **Codex (`codex exec --json`) as the second adapter (3.1), chosen BECAUSE it fits the contract badly rather than well. Five gaps, each declared instead of papered over: no live gauge (usage arrives only on `turn.completed`, after the session has ended), so `capabilities.usage` is false and the threshold policy is refused; no channel into a running exec, so `nudge` is false; no per-tool permission rules (codex speaks a sandbox enum and an approval policy), so a new capability `permission_rules` is false and the driver WARNS that the run's recorded allow/deny did nothing; no cost in the transport, so a new capability `cost` is false and the driver warns that `--cost-cap` can never fire; and no sofar MCP server in codex's config, so the pin line hands the session the CLI dialect (`sofar event append <slug> --source codex`) instead of tool names. The session id is ASSIGNED by the adapter — minted, written into the pin line, and reported on exit — never observed, and `resolveLaunchedSession` believes it only because the record registered it. `approval_policy=never` on every launch, and an unmappable permission mode throws instead of launching.** over opencode (also installed) as the second adapter; declaring `usage: true` on the strength of `turn.completed` and letting the threshold policy run on a gauge that only reads after the fact; silently dropping the allow-list that codex cannot express; letting `--cost-cap` sit silently inert; having the driven session mint its own session id; and mapping an unknown permission mode to a safe default rather than refusing because An adapter that fits perfectly proves nothing — it only shows the contract works for the agent it was written from. Codex disagrees with Claude Code on every axis the contract abstracts, so `sofar drive` running against it unchanged is the actual proof. Each gap is declared rather than worked around because a capability the driver cannot see is a capability the operator discovers by watching an unattended run fail to stop: a threshold policy on a post-hoc number would nudge nothing and hand off on the wrong reason, a cost cap that never fires is worse than no cost cap, and a recorded allow-list that had no effect is the exact overstatement session-driver D8's rule forbids. The assigned session id keeps D3 intact — the driver still refuses to believe any id the fold has not registered, so an id the session ignored falls through to the tool-and-time diff, which is the path Claude Code's hook-supplied id never exercised. Verified empirically against codex-cli 0.136.0 rather than assumed: the stream shapes were captured from a real `codex exec --json` pointed at an unreachable provider (zero API cost), the TokenUsage field names from the binary and a real rollout file, and the closed-stdin requirement from codex printing "Reading additional input from stdin" when stdin is a pipe.
- 2026-08-30T04:40:33.299Z — chose **Per-task routing lives on the TASK in the plan and loses to the run (3.2). A plan task gains `route {agent?, model?, effort?}` (schema `TaskRoute`, folded onto TaskState, rendered in plan.md); `sofar drive` resolves it per launch against a name→adapter map the CLI supplies, so the loop still knows no adapter names. Precedence is run-over-task: anything the RUN states — the recorded `run_started.surface` model/effort, or the driver's own --model/--effort — wins over a task hint, and the hint only fills what the run left open. Nothing new is recorded: the hint is already in the plan and `session_started.tool`/`model` already say what actually ran, so no handoff or run_started field asserts a route. Every routing failure is a PREFLIGHT refusal before run_started — an agent name the run cannot reach, or a routed adapter that cannot run the run's policy (threshold on an adapter with no gauge) — and every routing hint that is inert (overridden by the run, or unhonourable by its target adapter's capabilities.model/effort) is stated on the progress stream before the first launch.** over A task hint that overrides the run's recorded surface (the specific-wins default); recording the effective route on `handoff` or a second adapter name on `run_started`; a routing table in a config file or bindings.json rather than on the task; and a silent fallback to the default adapter when a route cannot be reached. because A hint that beat `run_started.surface` would make a resumed run two runs wearing one id — the record would name one model while half the sessions ran another, which is exactly the overstatement D8 forbids; run-over-task keeps the record's own words true and still leaves the plan free to route every task the run did not pin. Recording the route on the handoff would be the driver asserting a derived fact (D3): the plan carries the input and the session carries the outcome, and a third copy is the one that goes stale. Routing on the task rather than in a config file is D2's rule — the record is the queue, so the queue's entries carry their own routing and a resumed run reads them from the same fold. And a silent fallback is the trap D9 names: an unattended run that quietly runs a codex-routed task on Claude Code, or a threshold run whose routed session has no gauge, is discovered from the bill or from the transcript rather than from the driver, so it refuses to start instead.</because>
<parameter name="rule">A per-task `route` never overrides what the run recorded, and a route the run cannot reach or whose adapter cannot run the run's policy refuses the run before `run_started` — never a silent fallback to the default adapter.
